analysis.one_liner: Repeals Clean Air Act rules on toxic air emissions from industrial polluters.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Tom DeLay's bill would have deleted Section 112 of the Clean Air Act, the part that requires the EPA to list hazardous air pollutants and set emission limits for them. That section is the legal basis for federal limits on toxic chemicals released by refineries, chemical plants, and other industrial facilities. Wiping it out would have removed those federal limits entirely, leaving toxic air pollution to whatever rules states chose to impose.
analysis.who_benefits: Industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants — chemical plants, oil refineries, and similar operations — would be freed from federal emission standards, the compliance equipment those standards require, and the enforcement that comes with them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Industrial polluters like chemical plants and refineries

how_it_helps.text: Repealing Section 112 would eliminate the federal requirement to list hazardous air pollutants and set emission standards for them, ending the Clean Air Act's toxic air program entirely [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living near and downwind of industrial facilities would bear the cost, in the form of higher exposure to toxic air pollutants and loss of a federal backstop currently enforced by the EPA.

drawbacks.text: The bill offered no replacement protections: it simply repealed the hazardous air pollutant program with no substitute federal or guaranteed state standards, so health protections would depend entirely on individual states' willingness and capacity to regulate [S2][S3].

Section 112 standards impose real compliance costs on factories and refineries, and an honest supporter of repeal would have to acknowledge that the savings come from removing emission controls rather than from making them more efficient.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a straightforward repeal: polluters save the cost of controlling toxic emissions, and the public absorbs the health risk of unregulated toxic air. There was no offsetting benefit to ordinary people anywhere in the bill's text.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
On February 6, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it stayed for the rest of the 104th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor and never advanced beyond the subcommittee referral [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal toxic air pollution protections remained in place because the repeal never moved; the public kept Section 112's safeguards, and industrial emitters did not get the relief the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, because the repeal died

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act's hazardous air pollutant provisions.

for.name: 1 House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it drew.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee and never reported it out for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with a single Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support on record; the 104th Congress's Republican-led Commerce Committee let it die without action.

industries.note: These industries are the primary sources of the hazardous air pollutants covered by Section 112; repealing the emission standards would lift federal controls and their compliance costs. The public cost is greater exposure to toxic air emissions near and downwind of their facilities.
Firms that sell pollution-control technology to industrial facilities would lose the demand created by federal emission standards.
